things.label: Foreign passage
things.description: A passage containing a word with more than one plausible translation.

things.label: Bilingual glossary
things.description: Candidate correspondences between languages, useful but insufficient without context.

things.label: Collation
things.description: The copies preserve different words in the same passage. Collation puts the alternatives beside one another without deciding that the oldest-looking copy must be right.

things.label: Variant table
things.description: A quoted opening phrase—the lemma—identifies the passage being discussed. This reconstruction does not give ancient Alexandrian commentary modern line numbers.

things.label: Textual family
things.description: Shared copying errors suggest relationships between these copies. This is the modern curator's tentative family reconstruction; borrowing between copies can defeat a simple tree.

things.label: Reconstructed reading
things.description: The missing reading is proposed from the surviving variants and copying patterns. It remains a reconstruction, not recovered certainty, and is visibly marked as such.

things.label: Critical text
things.description: The editor distinguishes readable text from conjecture. A small uncertainty mark prevents the restoration from masquerading as an untouched ancient witness.

things.label: Critical edition
things.description: The text is accompanied by alternatives and explanations. Readers can inspect the editorial judgment rather than being asked to trust a silently repaired passage.

things.label: Draft translation
things.description: The first translation chooses one meaning for an ambiguous word. Its fluency is useful, but does not prove it preserved every implication of the source.

things.label: Annotated translation
things.description: A note explains the rejected meaning and why the context favored this one. The translation now exposes an interpretive decision instead of hiding it.

things.label: Parallel edition
things.description: Source text and translation can be compared passage by passage. The parallel edition gives readers a way to disagree with the translator.

cacheNarrative.label: A book with several pasts: collection
cacheNarrative.narrative: The collection contains variant manuscripts, damaged leaves, a bilingual glossary and correspondence.

args: Voluntary end of sitting after completing stage 3, not the campaign ending and not a technical block. 33 attempts, 27 accepted, 25 creations, 2 advances. Opening pots gave scientific-method labels a concrete anchor; calibration limits, retaining variation and repeatability allowing disagreement were worthwhile. Early plausible combinations failed with no explanation; empty hints felt like dead-end declarations although later-created partners worked. Stage 2 was smoother and I explored ambiguity/context beyond the goals because equal payments versus equal sacrifice mattered. The valid-argument output switched from levy fairness premises to a different rule-R example, weakening continuity. Stage 3 taught the useful caveat that copying between manuscripts can defeat a simple family tree, but supplied no actual variant words or foreign word to judge. I increasingly felt I was assembling labels for intellectual work rather than doing that work. Ending this sitting because the term-plus-modifier chains have become routine. Mild curiosity about later topics remains, but no strong immediate desire to return. Logical interface only; no graphics or touch assessment.
